style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 4 hands wisdom down three generations: Solomon recalls how his own father David taught him as a tender, beloved boy (vv. 1-9), and passes that same charge on to his sons -- 'get wisdom' as the one indispensable purchase, prized and embraced like a bride who crowns the one who loves her. The middle section sets the two roads side by side: the path of the righteous, brightening like dawn toward full day, against the way of the wicked, who stumble in a darkness they cannot even name (vv. 10-19). The chapter closes by guarding the four gates of the body -- heart, mouth, eyes, and feet -- because the heart is the wellspring from which the whole of life flows (vv. 20-27).

1.text: Listen, my sons, to a father's discipline; pay close attention, that you may come to know true understanding.
1.amp: Hear [shama -- listen so as to heed and obey], my sons [ben], the instruction [musar -- corrective discipline] of a father [ab], and pay attention [qashab -- prick up the ear, lean in hard] to know [yada] understanding [binah -- discernment].
1.notes: musar (H4148) is formative correction, not bare information; qashab (H7181) is the alert, leaning-in listening that refuses to miss a word. The plural 'sons' opens a new lecture, and the goal named is binah (H998), the trained power to tell one thing from another.

2.text: For what I give you is sound teaching -- do not abandon my instruction.
2.amp: For I give [natan] you good [tov -- beneficial, fitting] doctrine [leqach -- what is taken in and learned]; do not forsake [azab -- let go of, abandon] my law [torah -- instruction, teaching].
2.notes: leqach (H3948) is 'what is grasped,' the teachable substance a learner receives (cf. 1:5). torah (H8451) here is fatherly instruction carrying the same weight as the Law itself; azab (H5800) is a deliberate forsaking, the verb for abandoning a covenant.

3.text: For I too was a son to my father, tender in years, the cherished and only child in my mother's eyes.
3.amp: For I was a son [ben] to my father [ab], tender [rak -- soft, young, vulnerable] and the only [yachid -- only one, uniquely beloved] child in the sight [panim -- face, presence] of my mother [em].
3.notes: Solomon roots his authority in memory: he speaks not as a distant sage but as a son who was once taught. rak (H7390) is the soft tenderness of childhood; yachid (H3173) is the only/beloved one -- the same word used of Isaac, Abraham's only son (Gen 22:2).

4.text: He taught me, and said: 'Let your heart hold fast to my words; keep my commandments, and you will live.
4.amp: He taught [yarah -- instruct, point the way, as one aims an arrow] me, and said [amar] to me, 'Let your heart [leb] retain [tamak -- grasp firmly, hold up and sustain] my words [dabar]; keep [shamar -- guard, watch over] my commandments [mitsvah], and live [chayah -- be alive, truly live].'
4.notes: yarah (H3384) -- the root behind torah -- means to aim and direct, like an archer; tamak (H8551) is to take firm hold and sustain. The promise 'and live' (chayah, H2421) sets the keynote of the chapter: wisdom is not ornament but life itself (cf. v.13, v.22).

5.text: Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget, and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth.
5.amp: Get [qanah -- acquire, buy, make your own] wisdom [chokmah -- skill in living], get [qanah] understanding [binah]; do not forget [shakach] it, neither swerve [natah -- bend or turn away] from the words [emer] of my mouth [peh].
5.notes: qanah (H7069) is to acquire by purchase or labor -- wisdom is bought, not stumbled upon, and the urgent doubled imperative drives that home. natah (H5186), to bend aside, warns that drifting is as deadly as forgetting; both turn the heart off the straight line of the father's words.

6.text: Hold on to her and she will watch over you; cherish her and she will stand guard around you.
6.amp: Do not forsake [azab] her, and she will preserve [shamar -- keep, guard] you; love [ahab -- desire, delight in] her, and she will keep watch over [natsar -- guard, protect] you.
6.notes: Wisdom is personified as a woman to be loved and held fast -- the wholesome counterpart to the 'strange woman' of chapter 2. The guard-verbs shamar (H8104) and natsar (H5341) promise that the wisdom a man keeps will, in turn, keep him; ahab (H157) makes the relationship one of affection, not mere duty.

7.text: The first thing of all is wisdom -- so get wisdom; and with everything you gain, gain understanding.
7.amp: Wisdom [chokmah] is the beginning [reshith -- the head, the chief and first thing]; therefore get [qanah] wisdom, and with all your getting [qinyan -- all you acquire] get understanding [binah].
7.notes: reshith (H7225) means both 'first in importance' and 'the starting point' (cf. 1:7's reshith of knowledge). The verse insists wisdom is worth the whole price of a man's acquisitions -- whatever else he buys, let understanding be the purchase that orders the rest.

8.text: Prize her highly, and she will lift you up; she will bring you honor when you hold her close.
8.amp: Exalt [salal -- raise up, build up as one banks a highway] her, and she will promote [rum -- lift high, exalt] you; she will bring you to honor [kabad -- weight, glory, dignity] when you embrace [chabaq -- clasp, fold in your arms] her.
8.notes: salal (H5549) pictures raising a causeway -- esteem wisdom and she will raise you in turn; rum (H7311) answers it with God's own lifting up. kabad (H3513) carries the idea of 'weight' -- to honor is to give substance and glory. chabaq (H2263) is the embrace of a beloved, the warm clasp of one who treasures what he holds.

9.text: She will set a graceful wreath upon your head; a crown of splendor she will bestow on you.'
9.amp: She will give [natan] to your head [rosh] an ornament [livyah -- a wreath, a garland] of grace [chen -- favor, beauty]; a crown [atarah -- diadem, wreath] of glory [tipheret -- splendor, beauty] she will deliver to you.'
9.notes: livyah chen (H3880 + H2580) is the garland of favor a king or honored guest would wear (cf. 1:9). atarah (H5850) is the festal or royal crown, and tipheret (H8597) is radiant beauty -- wisdom's reward is not hidden gain but visible, public honor that adorns the one who holds her.

10.text: Hear, my son, and take my words to heart, and the years of your life will be many.
10.amp: Hear [shama], O my son [ben], and receive [laqach -- take to yourself, accept] my sayings [emer]; and the years [shanah] of your life [chay] shall be many [rabah -- be multiplied, increased].
10.notes: laqach (H3947) is more than hearing -- it is taking the words into one's own possession. The promise of multiplied years (rabah, H7235) is the standard wisdom-blessing: a life ordered by wisdom tends toward length and flourishing (cf. 3:2, 3:16).

11.text: I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you along straight paths.
11.amp: I have taught [yarah -- instruct, aim, point the way] you in the way [derek -- road, the pattern of a life] of wisdom [chokmah]; I have led [darak -- tread, set you walking, as one bends a bow] you in straight [yosher -- upright, level] paths [magal -- tracks, well-worn ruts].
11.notes: yarah (H3384) and darak (H1869) pair teaching with leading -- the father not only points the road but walks the son onto it. yosher (H3476) is straightness, the moral 'true line'; the metaphor of the way (derek, H1870) now governs the rest of the chapter's two-roads contrast.

12.text: When you walk, your stride will not be cramped, and if you run, you will not stumble.
12.amp: When you go [yalak -- walk, journey], your steps [tsaad -- stride, footfall] shall not be straitened [tsarar -- be hemmed in, cramped, made narrow]; and when you run [ruts -- rush, hurry], you shall not stumble [kashal -- totter and fall].
12.notes: tsarar (H3334) is to be hemmed into a tight, narrow place; the straight path of wisdom is open and unobstructed, room enough to walk and even to run. kashal (H3782), to stumble, becomes a key word in this chapter -- the wise walk free of it (v.12) while the wicked are defined by it (vv. 16, 19).

13.text: Take firm hold of discipline; do not let her go. Guard her well, for she is your life.
13.amp: Take fast hold [chazaq -- grip tightly, seize, hold with strength] of instruction [musar -- corrective discipline]; do not let her go [raphah -- loosen, slacken, let drop]; keep [natsar -- guard, watch over] her, for she is your life [chay].
13.notes: chazaq (H2388) is a strong, deliberate grip; raphah (H7503) is its opposite, the slackening hand that lets a thing slip away. To call musar (H4148) 'your life' (chay, H2416) raises discipline above mere advice -- the correction a man clings to is the very thing keeping him alive.

14.text: Do not set foot on the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of evildoers.
14.amp: Do not enter [bo -- come into, set foot in] the path [orach -- way, road] of the wicked [rasha -- guilty, lawless], and do not walk [ashar -- go straight on, advance] in the way [derek] of evil [ra -- harmful, wicked] men.
14.notes: the warning turns from the bright road to the dark one. orach (H734) and derek (H1870) are paired ways; rasha (H7563) is the legally guilty, the one in the wrong before God. The command is total -- not merely 'do not live there' but 'do not even step onto it.'

15.text: Steer clear of it; do not travel on it. Turn away from it and pass on by.
15.amp: Avoid [para -- let it loose, leave it behind] it, do not pass [abar -- cross over, go along] by it; turn aside [satah -- swerve away] from it, and pass on [abar].
15.notes: five sharp imperatives crowd this short verse, hammering the same point: avoid, do not pass, turn, pass on. abar (H5674) means to cross over and move past -- the wise man does not linger to inspect the evil road but turns from it and keeps going.

16.text: For they cannot sleep unless they have done some harm; their rest is robbed from them until they have made someone fall.
16.amp: For they do not sleep [yashen] unless they have done evil [raa -- act wickedly, do harm]; their sleep [shenah] is taken away [gazal -- seized, torn away by force] unless they make someone stumble [kashal -- fall].
16.notes: gazal (H1497) is violent seizure -- their very sleep is robbed from them, so consumed are they with mischief. The wicked are driven men: harm is not an occasional lapse but an appetite they must feed before they can rest, and the word kashal (H3782) ties their craving to the downfall of others.

17.text: They feed on the bread of wickedness and drink down the wine of violence.
17.amp: For they eat [lacham -- consume; the root also means to wage war] the bread [lechem] of wickedness [resha -- wrongdoing, moral evil], and drink [shatah] the wine [yayin] of violence [chamas -- brutality, injustice].
17.notes: the metaphor makes evil their daily diet -- wickedness is their bread, violence their wine, the very sustenance they live on. chamas (H2555) is cruel, lawless violence; there is a grim pun in lacham (H3898), 'to eat,' whose root also means 'to do battle' -- their food is their warfare.

18.text: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until the full light of day.
18.amp: But the path [orach] of the just [tsaddiq -- righteous, in the right] is like the shining [nogah -- radiance, glow] light [or]; that shines [or -- gives light] more and more [halak -- going on, advancing] to the perfect [kun -- established, firmly set] day [yom].
18.notes: set in stark contrast to v.16-17: the righteous road brightens like sunrise climbing toward noon. nogah (H5051) is the growing glow of dawn; kun (H3559), 'the established day,' is the noontide when the light stands full and firm. The righteous life is a gradual, ever-increasing illumination.

19.text: The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not even know what makes them stumble.
19.amp: The way [derek] of the wicked [rasha] is like darkness [aphelah -- thick gloom, calamity]; they do not know [yada] at what they stumble [kashal -- fall].
19.notes: aphelah (H653) is the densest darkness, the gloom of calamity. The tragedy is not only that the wicked fall but that they walk blind -- they cannot even name what trips them. Where the righteous see more clearly with every step (v.18), the wicked grope in a dark they do not recognize.

20.text: My son, give heed to my words; bend your ear to what I say.
20.amp: My son [ben], attend [qashab -- listen intently, prick up the ear] to my words [dabar]; incline [natah -- stretch, bend toward] your ear [ozen] to my sayings [emer].
20.notes: the closing section opens, like v.1, with a summons to listen -- qashab (H7181) and the inclined ear (ozen, H241) ask the whole posture of attention. natah (H5186), to bend toward, is the same verb warned against in v.5 ('do not swerve'): here the son is to bend his ear the right direction, toward the father's words.

21.text: Do not let them slip from your sight; keep them deep within your heart.
21.amp: Let them not depart [luz -- turn aside, slip away] from your eyes [ayin]; keep [shamar -- guard, preserve] them in the midst [tavek -- the center, the inmost part] of your heart [lebab].
21.notes: luz (H3868) is to turn aside or slip off the line -- the words must stay fixed before the eyes, not drift. To keep them in the tavek (H8432), the very center of the lebab (H3824), prepares for v.23: the heart is the controlling core, and what is guarded there governs everything.

22.text: For they are life to those who find them, and healing to their whole body.
22.amp: For they are life [chay] to those who find [matsa -- discover, attain] them, and health [marpe -- healing, a cure, medicine] to all their flesh [basar -- body, the whole physical self].
22.notes: matsa (H4672), to find, recalls the treasure-search of chapter 2 -- the words are a discovery worth seeking. marpe (H4832) is healing or medicine (the marginal Hebrew literally reads 'medicine'); wisdom is not only spiritual but bodily wholeness, life and health for the whole basar (H1320).

23.text: Above everything you guard, guard your heart, for from it flow the springs of life.
23.amp: Keep [natsar -- guard, watch over] your heart [leb] with all diligence [mishmar -- above all keeping, more than any guarded post]; for out of it are the issues [totsaah -- outgoings, the boundaries from which streams flow] of life [chay].
23.notes: the chapter's summit. The Hebrew literally reads 'above all keeping, guard your heart' -- mishmar (H4929) is a guard-post, and the heart (leb, H3820) is the one above all to be watched. totsaah (H8444) names the source-springs or outlets: the heart is the wellspring, and every stream of word, eye, and step that follows flows out from it.

24.text: Put away from you a crooked mouth, and keep deceitful lips far from you.
24.amp: Put away [sur -- turn aside, remove] from you a perverse [iqqesh -- twisted, crooked] mouth [peh], and perverse [lazuth -- deviousness, crookedness] lips [saphah] put far [rachaq -- keep distant, banish] from you.
24.notes: the first gate beyond the heart is the mouth. iqqesh (H6143) is the twisted-out-of-true crookedness; the Hebrew margin reads 'frowardness of mouth and perverseness of lips.' What the heart guards, the speech reveals -- so the crooked mouth is removed (sur, H5493) and banished far (rachaq, H7368) from the wise man.

25.text: Let your eyes look straight ahead; fix your gaze directly before you.
25.amp: Let your eyes [ayin] look [nabat -- gaze, regard attentively] straight ahead [nokach -- in front, opposite, directly forward], and let your eyelids [aphaph -- the eyelids, the glance] look straight [yashar -- be straight, level] before you.
25.notes: the gate of the eyes. nabat (H5027) is a fixed, deliberate gaze, and nokach (H5227) is dead-ahead -- the wise eye does not wander toward the forbidden road of v.14. yashar (H3474), to make straight, ties the look of the eye to the straight paths of v.11: vision and direction are one.

26.text: Make level the track for your feet, and let all your ways be firmly set.
26.amp: Ponder [palas -- weigh, make level, lay out straight] the path [magal -- track, course] of your feet [regel], and let all your ways [derek] be established [kun -- firmly set, made secure].
26.notes: the gate of the feet. palas (H6424) means both to weigh thoughtfully and to make level -- consider your course and grade it smooth. kun (H3559) is the same 'established' as the 'perfect day' of v.18: a deliberately weighed path becomes a firmly settled life, ordered aright.

27.text: Veer aside neither rightward nor leftward; pull your foot back from whatever is evil.
27.amp: Do not turn [natah -- bend, swerve] to the right hand [yamin] nor to the left [semol]; remove [sur -- turn aside, take away] your foot [regel] from evil [ra -- harm, wickedness].
27.notes: the chapter ends as it ran -- on the straight line. natah (H5186), the swerving verb of v.5 and v.21, is now forbidden in either direction: no deviation right or left from the level path. sur (H5493) echoes v.24's 'put away'; the foot, like the mouth, is turned decisively away from ra (H7451), evil.
